human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper presents a coherent, well-engineered transition-based neural parser that jointly generates nodes, alignments and graph transitions with an arc-eager variant, pointer-network hard attention, stack-conditioned encoder lookups, and delexicalized predicate handling. Empirical ablations support that arc-eager + hard attention + stack features materially improve DMRS/EDS DEV-set EDM. The batched, static-graph transition executor is a valuable engineering contribution enabling high GPU throughput.

Strengths: Clear mapping from representation needs to model decisions; systematic ablations across linearizations and attention modes; practical GPU-batched transition implementation with demonstrated throughput gains; cross-representation evaluation exposing alignment-sensitivity.

Limitations: (1) Headline numeric provenance is incomplete (e.g., 86.69% Smatch claim); without explicit mapping to experiments/evaluation scripts these claims are hard to validate. (2) Alignment-supervision heterogeneity (gold for DeepBank vs JAMR automatic for AMR) is a central confound: benefits of hard-attention may partly reflect gold alignment availability. (3) Throughput claims compare GPU-batched neural runs to CPU ACE with differing coverage settings—hardware and coverage mismatches complicate the claimed order-of-magnitude speed advantage. (4) Oracle representability (~98-99%) is asserted but not fully documented by per-representation breakdowns or failure examples, weakening the 'full-coverage' phrasing.

Open Questions: (1) Please provide the experiment mapping that yields every headline number and release the evaluation scripts so readers can reproduce reported metrics. (2) How does performance of hard-attention models degrade with alignment noise? Provide controlled gold/noisy alignment experiments and matched soft-attention baselines. (3) Provide oracle-extraction details and per-representation coverage breakdowns with example non-representable graphs. (4) Re-run or augment throughput comparisons to ensure hardware/coverage parity (neural CPU-only timings, ACE on comparable hardware, batch-size sensitivity curves).

Transparency: Reviewers repeatedly request code/evaluation scripts, hardware details, alignment preprocessing scripts (JAMR/CoreNLP/ERG lexicon versions), oracle-extraction code, and tests showing batched decoding equals single-instance outputs. Inclusion of these artifacts and added experimental controls will substantially increase reproducibility and resolve the principal epistemic uncertainties.

confidence_interval.rationale: Reviewers express moderate-to-high confidence that the core empirical claims within the authors' experimental regime are valid: arc-eager + pointer + stack improves DMRS/EDS DEV EDM and batched static-graph execution yields high GPU throughput. Uncertainties lower the top bound due to missing provenance for headline figures, heterogeneous alignment supervision confounding architecture claims (MRS vs AMR), and fairness issues in throughput comparisons versus ACE; resolving these would increase confidence further.

Graph-based parsers (McDonald, 2006) treat pars- ing as a search-based structured prediction prob- lem in which the goal is learning a scoring func- tion over dependency trees such that the correct tree is scored above all other trees. Transition-based parsers (Nivre, 2004; Nivre, 2008) treat parsing as a sequence of actions that produce a parse tree, and a classiﬁer is trained to score the possible actions at each stage of the process and guide the parsing pro- cess. Perhaps the simplest graph-based parsers are arc-factored (ﬁrst order) models (McDonald, 2006), in which the scoring function for a tree decomposes over the individual arcs of the tree. More elaborate models look at larger (overlapping) parts, requiring more sophisticated inference and training algorithms (Martins et al., 2009; Koo and Collins, 2010). The basic transition-based parsers work in a greedy man- ner, performing a series of locally-optimal decisions, and boast very fast parsing speeds. More advanced transition-based parsers introduce some search into the process using a beam (Zhang and Clark, 2008) or dynamic programming (Huang and Sagae, 2010). Speciﬁcally, we exploit Freebase, a large community-authored knowledge base that spans many sub-domains and stores real world facts in graphical format, and parsed sentences from a large corpus. Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
